articles.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother will make you forget all about Marvel’s Blade disaster
articles.text:
Marvel’s mishandling of its Blade reboot will likely go down as one of the studio’s biggest mistakes. There was a great actor in place to play the vampire hunter (Mahershala Ali), and a promising director set to take over the reins (Bassam Tariq). In retrospect, though, the disappointing demise of Blade might not be such a bad thing, because Tariq and Ali have collaborated on something much more interesting than a superhero reboot: the powerful hitman thriller Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.
Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother will make you forget all about Marvel’s Blade disaster
Reviews from TIFF 2026: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, In Alaska, The Face of Horror, Babies, and Drifter.
That was one of five movies I was able to cram into a very hectic third day at the Toronto International Film Festival (you can see my previous reports here and here), and it was one of those days that drives home why events like TIFF can be so special. Each film I saw was drastically different from the last — there was everything from a drama about drifting cars to a throwback horror flick based on a famous Japanese ghost story — which was a great reminder that there are still plenty of new ideas left in the world of film.
So let’s get to it. Here are some rapid-fire reviews of everything I saw on day 3 at TIFF.
Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother
In theaters in October
Latif (Ali) lives a life of contradictions: he’s a devout Muslim and loyal father, but he also works as a hitman, albeit one who works under a specific moral code (only kill bad guys; never use a gun). But both his faith and his code are tested when his wife dies and he’s forced to become a single father to three kids, including a newborn baby. At the same time, his blood-soaked past comes back to haunt him, putting everyone at risk. We’re in a great moment for pure action flicks like Furious or the John Wick franchise, but Your Mother offers something very different. It’s a powerful character study, one where the action is comparatively fleeting, but all the more powerful and impactful because of it. It’s a film that always left me guessing just how Latif was going to get through this, and, despite being very serious and often solemn, the story also has plenty of laugh-out-loud moments. Ali is excellent as the morally questionable righteous killer, but I was also really impressed by John Cho as the villain, a charismatically unhinged leader of a right-wing church group.
In Alaska
No theatrical date yet
A slow-burning crime thriller, In Alaska, co-directed by Jaap van Heusden and Vinnie Karetak., follows a suicidal teen named Woody (Leo Matthew Temela) who, after a tragic mishap, finds himself wanted by the FBI for causing millions of dollars worth of damage to an oil pipeline. It’s a film of two sides: Woody’s desperate attempts at survival, and veteran agent Susan (Noomi Rapace), the only who realizes the damage wasn’t caused by eco-terrorists. In Alaska is a moodier take on the genre, and one that asks some difficult and important questions about both its leads, particularly Woody, who constantly grapples with whether he even wants to live at all. What starts out bleak ends on a much more hopeful note.
The Face of Horror
No theatrical date yet
Conceptually, Anna Biller’s The Face of Horror is a mishmash of styles and influences. It’s based on the influential Japanese ghost story Yotsuya Kaidan, but adapts the tale for 14th century England. It then renders the whole thing in the style of Technicolor horror classics. That curious combination works, though, as the film has a campy sense of theatricality to it, with over-the-top performances and classic-style special effects — including some truly memorable make-up work — that lend its grisly tale of murder and betrayal a distinct vibe. And it’s all held together by two strong lead performances: Eleanor (Kristine Froseth), the jilted wife-turned-nightmare of Edward (Jonah Hauer-King), a smarmy and morally-dubious knight who is the kind of asshole you can’t wait to see get what’s coming to him.
Babies
No theatrical date yet
A film that explores that nagging question many long-term couples are forced to answer repeatedly: when are you going to have a baby? Written and directed by Lauren Miller Rogen, Babies is centered on Annie (Anna Kendrick) and Aaron (Seth Rogen), the only childless couple in their social circle. But Annie can’t stop thinking about the question — there’s a lot of her internal monologue debating the pros and cons of having kids — and the couple are forced to really confront the idea when a close friend and her young daughter come to stay with them, providing a taste of parenthood. Babies works for two reasons. First, it’s hilarious: Kendrick and Rogen have a blast together, and the supporting cast includes the likes of Issa Rae, Zach Cherry, and Ed Helm. But it also feels grounded in a way that makes it very relatable, whether you have kids or not.
Drifter
No theatrical date yet
If Good Will Hunting and The Fast and the Furious were smushed together, you might get something like Drifter. The film is directed by longtime Fast star Sung Kang, who also plays the lead role of Tree, the janitor of a smalltown race track who moonlights as a driver for a drug kingpin. But all he really wants to do is drift, and events conspire to bring him to an event where he’ll go up against the best drifters in the world. The challenges are much more than just on the track, though; Tree has spent most of his life alone, so he’s forced to learn to open up to others, and he also has to contend with extracting himself from the world of crime. Unfortunately, Drifter leans too heavily on the established formula of underdog sports stories, which makes most of its beats feel predictable, with the exception of its completely improbable ending. Worse still is that, with the exception of Tree, none of the characters feel developed at all, and the crime thriller aspect doesn’t gel well with the feel-good story. At least there are some beautiful sequences that make drifting a car feel like an artform.

articles.title: Từ mượn sổ đỏ vay nợ, người phụ nữ miền Tây dựng cơ sở cá thát lát thu 28 tỷ/năm
articles.text:
Từ những lần trắng tay đến thương hiệu cá thát lát tiền tỷ
Bà Nguyễn Kim Thùy (52 tuổi, ngụ xã Thạnh Hòa, TP Cần Thơ) sinh ra trong một gia đình nông dân đông anh em. Năm 1993, một năm sau khi lập gia đình, bà khởi nghiệp bằng nghề nuôi cá trê lai.
Không có vốn, vợ chồng bà phải mượn sổ đỏ của ông nội chồng để vay 2,5 triệu đồng. Sau 3 tháng, lứa cá đầu tiên bán được 6 triệu đồng. Trả hết nợ, số tiền còn lại bà làm vốn để tiếp tục nuôi cá.
Thấy nghề nuôi cá trê thuận lợi, bà quyết định đầu tư lớn. Bà dốc toàn bộ tiền tích lũy, mượn ao của người thân và vay ngân hàng hơn 500 triệu đồng để mở rộng quy mô. Tận dụng phần ruộng của cha mẹ ruột, vợ chồng bà tự tay cải tạo thành ao nuôi.
“Chồng dùng len đào đất, còn tôi đứng dưới chuyền, thảy đất lên. Anh em trong dòng họ cũng phụ giúp. Người ta đào ao bằng máy móc chỉ 1-2 ngày là xong, còn vợ chồng tôi làm bằng tay nên mất cả tháng”, bà Thùy nhớ lại.
Nhưng khi quy mô nuôi ngày càng lớn, biến cố bất ngờ xảy ra. Cá mắc bệnh, chết hàng loạt khiến vốn liếng gần như mất sạch. Đến hạn đáo hạn, ngân hàng không tiếp tục cho vay, gia đình bà phải chạy vạy lo trả nợ.
Trong lúc khốn khó, điều bà nhớ nhất không phải số tiền đã mất mà là sự giúp đỡ của người thân.
Biết bà gặp khó, người thân trong gia đình mang sổ đỏ đến cho mượn để bà thế chấp ngân hàng vay tiền. Có người đưa vàng để bà xoay xở. “Hành động và tình cảm của người thân khiến tôi rất xúc động, trở thành động lực để mình tiếp tục phấn đấu”, bà Thùy nói.
Sau cú ngã đó, bà không bỏ cuộc mà tìm hướng khác để kiếm sống, vừa trang trải gia đình vừa lo cho các con ăn học.
Bà dựng một quán cà phê nhỏ trên phần đất của gia đình. Thấy bán cà phê thu nhập không đáng kể, bà chuyển sang mở quán ăn, rồi tự học cách chế biến món ăn theo yêu cầu và khẩu vị của khách.
Khách gọi những món bà chưa biết nấu như cá lóc, lươn, ếch, bà lại hỏi cách chế biến rồi làm thử. Mỗi người một khẩu vị, bà ghi nhớ rồi điều chỉnh món ăn cho phù hợp.
Quán ngày càng đông, có thời điểm quán phục vụ 30-40 bàn khách mỗi ngày. Vừa đi chợ vừa nấu ăn từ sáng đến tối, công việc vất vả khiến bà nhiều lúc kiệt sức. Vì thế, bà bắt đầu nghĩ đến việc tìm một công việc ổn định hơn.
Năm 2014, bà cùng chồng tính chuyện chuyển nghề. Chồng bà sang làm nghề lái cá tại chợ Bình Điền (TPHCM). Lần đầu buôn cá rô, do chưa có kinh nghiệm, bà chịu lỗ khoảng 200 triệu đồng. Không bỏ cuộc, bà rút kinh nghiệm rồi chuyển sang thu mua cá thát lát.
Đến năm 2015, khi giá cá thát lát giảm mạnh, chứng kiến người nuôi điêu đứng vì đầu ra bấp bênh, bà nhận ra nếu chỉ bán cá nguyên liệu thì người nông dân rất dễ rơi vào cảnh được mùa mất giá.
Từ đó, bà nảy ra ý tưởng chế biến sâu để nâng giá trị con cá thát lát.
Trước đó, một số món cá thát lát do bà chế biến tại quán đã được thực khách yêu thích. Người ăn tại quán mua về nhà, mang đi đãi tiệc rồi giới thiệu cho người khác. Đơn hàng vì thế tăng dần.
Không chỉ bán cá, phải làm chủ chuỗi giá trị
Dù chồng nhiều lần cằn nhằn vì sản lượng còn ít, bà vẫn quyết tâm đầu tư tiền làm bao bì, xét nghiệm mẫu, công bố sản phẩm để xây dựng thương hiệu riêng.
Năm 2015, bà đăng ký thương hiệu độc quyền cá thát lát Kỳ Như.
“Tôi nghĩ sản phẩm muốn phát triển thì phải có thương hiệu, phải làm bài bản”, bà Thùy chia sẻ.
Sản phẩm đầu tiên là cá thát lát muối sả còn xương. Trong quá trình bán hàng, bà nhận thấy người lớn tuổi và trẻ em gặp khó khăn khi ăn cá vì nhiều xương. Từ thực tế đó, bà bắt đầu nghiên cứu cách làm cá thát lát rút xương.
Bà thử nhiều cách chế biến, cho mọi người dùng thử rồi tiếp tục điều chỉnh công thức. Sản phẩm nào được thị trường đón nhận mới tiếp tục đầu tư sản xuất.
Từ một món ăn trong quán, cá thát lát dần trở thành sản phẩm hàng hóa.
Năm 2019, bà Thùy thành lập hợp tác xã (HTX). Từ 11 thành viên ban đầu, đến nay, HTX có 56 thành viên, với tổng diện tích vùng nuôi khoảng 17ha, trong đó gia đình bà có 5ha.
HTX cung ứng con giống, hỗ trợ kỹ thuật và bao tiêu sản phẩm cho người dân với mức giá ổn định, thường cao hơn giá thị trường khoảng 2.000-10.000 đồng/kg, theo bà Thùy.
Việc liên kết giúp người nuôi có đầu ra ổn định, trong khi HTX chủ động được nguồn nguyên liệu phục vụ chế biến.
Từ kinh nghiệm từng nhiều lần lao đao vì giá cá, bà Thùy đặc biệt chú trọng xây dựng chuỗi sản xuất khép kín, từ tuyển chọn cá bố mẹ, sản xuất con giống, nuôi thương phẩm đến chế biến. Quá trình nuôi được kiểm soát về nguồn nước, thức ăn, việc sử dụng thuốc thú y và tuân thủ quy định về kháng sinh.
HTX hiện có 11 sản phẩm đạt chuẩn OCOP, trong đó 10 sản phẩm 4 sao và một sản phẩm 5 sao cấp quốc gia là cá thát lát rút xương tẩm gia vị.
Sản phẩm của HTX Kỳ Như hiện có mặt tại khoảng 20 tỉnh, thành, được phân phối qua các hệ thống siêu thị và xuất khẩu sang Mỹ, Hàn Quốc. Theo bà Thùy, tổng doanh thu của cơ sở đạt khoảng 28 tỷ đồng/năm, lợi nhuận đạt vài tỷ đồng.
Nuôi cá trên cạn bằng bể nổi
Đầu năm 2026, bà tiếp tục đầu tư thử nghiệm mô hình nuôi cá thát lát trên cạn bằng bể nổi, kết hợp hệ thống lọc và xử lý nước. Mỗi bể có thể nuôi khoảng 5,5 tấn cá.
Theo bà, mô hình này giúp kiểm soát tốt nguồn nước, hạn chế dịch bệnh và đặc biệt phù hợp với những hộ có ít đất sản xuất. Nếu thành công, bà mong muốn có thể nhân rộng để người dân có thêm sinh kế.
Không chỉ đầu tư cho vùng nguyên liệu, bà còn chú trọng hiện đại hóa nhà máy. Nhiều công đoạn như đánh vảy, tách xương, quết chả, trộn gia vị, hấp, chiên, hút chân không có máy móc hỗ trợ.
HTX áp dụng các tiêu chuẩn ISO 22000:2018, HACCP, VietGAP, đầu tư kho bảo quản, hệ thống xử lý nước thải và từng bước tự động hóa sản xuất.
Tuy nhiên, bà không muốn tự động hóa hoàn toàn. Một số công đoạn như tách xương, xẻ cá, ướp cá vẫn được kết hợp thủ công để tạo việc làm cho phụ nữ địa phương.
Nhìn lại hơn 20 năm lập nghiệp, bà không xem những lần thất bại là điều đáng quên. Ngược lại, mỗi lần trắng tay lại cho bà thêm một bài học để bước tiếp.
Bà Thùy từng được bình chọn là nông dân sản xuất, kinh doanh giỏi toàn quốc và năm 2023 được Thủ tướng Chính phủ tặng Bằng khen.

articles.title: Try These 3 iOS 27 Safari Settings to Get More Out of Apple’s Browser
articles.text:
At Apple’s recent hardware event, the software powering its foldable iPhone Duo stood out, with translucent Liquid Glass effects and vertically stacked icons. But you don’t need to snatch a folding smartphone to reap the benefits of Apple’s iOS 27 updates.
When iOS 27 leaves beta on Monday, Siri AI’s standalone app and smartphone search integration will likely be the most immediately obvious change for many iPhone users. But it’s worth digging even deeper to uncover helpful additions to key apps, like Apple’s Safari browser, as well as revamps to underutilized apps, like Shortcuts.
The version of Safari available in iOS 27 looks fairly similar to the last iteration, with a few key updates tucked away in the settings. These Safari features are powered by Apple Intelligence, which requires an iPhone 15 Pro or newer (they're also available on iPadOS 27 and macOS 27).
Notify Me
If you’re shopping online and want a quick price-drop notification, you can use the “Notify Me” feature to scan a webpage on a certain cadence and look for changes. First, head to the page you want to track and tap the three-lined hamburger menu icon in the top right corner of Safari. About halfway down, you’ll see this option listed.
“Safari can let you know when a website updates the content you’re interested in,” reads the feature’s description. Here you’ll find an open text box where you can describe what change in content you want Safari to scan for, as well as how often you want it to check.
For example, my couch is broken, so I’ve been eyeing a few different replacement options. I have two final contenders from CB2, but both are out of my price range. So, I set up a “Notify Me” for Safari to scan the pages each day for a significant discount. Whichever one goes on sale first will likely be what I decide to get, and now I don’t have to refresh the pages manually every day.
While many other browsers have similar shopping features, like the price-tracking bell in Google Chrome, I appreciate how this feature stretches beyond just buying stuff. You can also use Safari to scan for ticket drops, privacy policy changes, and other content updates.
Describe an Extension
If you’ve experimented already with the “Describe a Shortcut” feature for iPhone automation, then “Describe an Extension” for Safari will seem familiar. It's located under the same settings menu as the “Notify Me” tool, just a little further down.
The feature asks you to type what you want the extension to do, then generates a custom option. Some of the suggested prompts in Safari revolve around boosting productivity, like “display a reading time estimate as a badge on the extension,” maintaining better focus, like “make the web page grayscale,” and more random ideas, like “show a colorful and explosive firework every time I tap.”
It took only a few seconds for each of those three examples to generate. Safari also suggests pre-made extensions during the process that could fit what you’re looking to do. As I scrolled through the internet with all three of the new extensions activated, everything worked as expected. While I’ll likely only keep the grayscale one to help me focus while reading online articles, the fireworks felt whimsical in small doses.
Organize Tabs
I am a glutton for mobile tabs, especially on Safari. I’m rarely ever exiting out of anything and always just pop open something new, which leaves me with hundreds upon hundreds of loosely connected, completely unorganized tabs—until now.
This feature is in the wider browser tab view accessible by tapping the two overlapping squares at the bottom-right corner of your screen. Swipe to a tab group brimming with websites and look for the three-lined button in the top-left. Here’s where you can choose to allow Safari to “automatically create topics” based on those tabs.
It takes a few seconds to organize everything after you activate this feature, but it did a great job of finding helpful trends in those 500+ tabs. For example, it grouped all the WIRED articles I had open and created a tab topic for upcoming San Francisco event pages and comedy clubs I was considering checking out.

articles.title: Are Apple's wired EarPods still worth buying? - Engadget
articles.text:
Are Apple's wired EarPods still worth buying?
Apple still sells its classic wired earbuds for a reason.
AirPods turn 10 this year, and they're everywhere now. They've also evolved over time; modern AirPods pack in noise cancellation, health sensors and even built-in live translation. If people ever had doubts about wireless earbuds, that's largely a concern of the past — though maybe not completely.
As it turns out, there's a niche group of people who still buy wired earbuds, like EarPods. Remember Apple's wired earbuds that used to come in the box with an iPhone? While using them now might seem like nothing more than nostalgia, there are a few reasons to prefer EarPods over AirPods.
What's different between AirPods and EarPods?
Comparing AirPods and EarPods isn't as simple as "wired versus wireless." AirPods are packed with modern features that make them go far beyond a simple pipe for transmitting audio. Take the AirPods Pro 3, for example, which can track your heart rate during a workout. There's also Spatial Audio and all the specs that make them sound great. In comparison, EarPods are just regular earbuds. They lack fancy gestures or voice commands.
Yet they can be better than AirPods in some ways. EarPods require zero maintenance. No battery means no charging, so they're ready whenever you are. Compare that to leaving your AirPods sitting off the charger for a few days and being greeted by a red battery icon. Having a cord also means zero pairing issues stemming from Bluetooth. There's no need to worry about re-pairing if you want to share your earbuds with a friend either.
The built-in EarPods microphone also delivers better voice quality. While Apple has done a good job of improving this aspect of AirPods, Bluetooth audio still doesn't sound as good as wired audio. They even come in three connection types: 3.5mm, Lightning and USB-C. That makes EarPods compatible with a wide range of gadgets, and they're cheap enough that you could buy separate pairs for different devices.
Due to the lack of a headphone jack on modern iPhones, though, using the Lightning or USB-C port for EarPods means you can't charge your phone while using your earbuds. If this poses a major issue for you, an adapter that splits the port into two is an easy fix, though it's not as convenient to carry around and have attached to your phone.
AirPods are better, but there's still room for EarPods
There's no denying that AirPods are better in many ways. Apple's wired earphones won't give you noise cancellation, which by itself is a compelling reason to choose AirPods. But sometimes you might prefer simplicity over high-end tech. Maybe you don't want to worry about recharging your earbuds, or perhaps yours always tend to die during an important meeting. Moments like this make it sensible to keep some wired earbuds around.
Then there's the price. The cheapest AirPods you can buy today cost $129, and they aren't even the best ones. For $19, EarPods are unbeatable. They aren't designed to be the best, but they cost a fraction of Apple's wireless earbuds. Maybe you'd rather spend $19 on EarPods than $69+ to replace your lost AirPod every six months. Or you can buy both and always have what the situation calls for.

articles.title: From IFA demonstrations to a wider design question: why should an office chair expect the body to stay still?
articles.text:
At IFA Berlin 2026, ARBREST put a chair through movements that office furniture often treats as exceptions. COVE is the new brand’s first product, made its world debut with an IFA Best of Design award. At Hall 2.2, Stand 141, visitors leaned toward a desk, shifted their shoulders, turned and reclined. The demonstration made a larger point: working is not a single posture, and support should not disappear when the body changes direction.
COVE is ARBREST’s first product and first expression of that idea in the ergonomic chair category. The new smart lifestyle technology brand focuses on real needs that remain poorly addressed in work and everyday life. Its aim is to let technology recede into the background. COVE is the brand’s first step, not a claim that ARBREST will only make ergonomic chairs.
The reason for developing the chair is closely connected to the limits of standard office furniture. Many chairs are built around a standardized reference body, with differences addressed later through adjustments. That approach can leave smaller users compensating for a seat that is too deep, a lumbar support out of reach, armrests too far apart or feet that do not land securely. Women’s bodies are not identical, but the category has often treated their proportions as an afterthought. ARBREST decided to make them an initial design reference.
COVE starts with a 7-Point Fit Calibration. Seat height, width and depth, lumbar support, armrests, headrest and footrest are considered together. The recommended user height is 150 to 175 centimetres; seat height ranges from 46 to 54 centimetres and seat depth from 43 to 49 centimetres. The idea is to establish a better fit from the start, rather than relying on adjustment to compensate for the wrong proportions.
The seat has its own logic. A firmer sit-bone zone provides a stable base. A contoured pelvic area follows the body’s shape, and a flexible front edge is intended to reduce pressure under the thighs. The dual-tier active footrest helps bridge the gap between leg length and seat height. Together, these details address a familiar problem: when the legs, pelvis and lower back do not share a stable base, the user keeps moving in search of one.
COVE’s other details are similarly grounded in ordinary habits. The 3D Winged Headrest creates clearance for ponytails and styled hair during recline. Wide-surface touch controls are intended to be easier with longer nails. The 5D armrests follow the elbows as the user types, reads, browses or turns to communicate. None of these features changes the category alone. Together, they suggest that the chair was designed around a person’s routine rather than an abstract diagram of correct sitting.
Movement becomes more visible in the mechanism. COVE’s multi-axis forward-tilt chassis reaches 16 degrees, allowing the user to move closer to the desk without perching on the seat edge. The footrest continues to support the legs. The point is not to demonstrate how much a chair can move, but to keep support present as the body leans forward, sits upright, turns or reclines.
The 12-Zone Micro-Motion Backrest distributes support across twelve independent units arranged along a flexible spine plate. A small turn of the shoulders, a change in weight or a shift in the lower back can be met by different areas of the backrest. This is a different answer to the familiar ergonomic instruction to “sit correctly.” Instead of holding the body still, the chair is designed to stay connected as the body moves.
COVE links that backrest to a 5-Point Synchronized Support system. The headrest, armrests, backrest, seat and footrest move as coordinated contact points. When fatigue appears, one touch activates the motorized lumbar support. As the backrest reclines, the support extends forward and the footrest continues to cradle the legs, creating a brief seated stretch.
The market value of this approach is not that COVE promises to solve every problem associated with desk work. It is that the chair gives a growing conversation about inclusive design a physical, testable form. Designing for women here means more than reducing dimensions. It means looking at where the pelvis settles, how the feet are supported, how hair and fingernails affect daily use, and how a person moves between concentration and rest.
After its IFA debut, ARBREST expects to move COVE into an initial launch or crowdfunding phase later in 2026. Launch details will be announced later. Its broader significance lies in its starting assumption: the user is not a fixed shape, and a chair should not require her to behave like one. COVE is the brand’s first product, and its first step toward further smart lifestyle products built around real user needs.
